name: Pad with a moving inner voice
rationale: A sustained open pad (a low fifth and a high root as a frame) with one inner voice that steps between chord tones every half bar or every beat, the way a string pad or a choir keeps a held chord alive. Today pads only hold one block chord per bar, so this adds slow movement without adding rhythm. The verse takes move once per half bar (one over four bars), the middle take moves on every beat, and the chorus take adds a high third on top.

name: Pumping sidechain pad
rationale: The pumping pad of house, EDM and dance pop: the chord ducks on every kick and swells back between them. The engine has no sidechain, so the pump is written into the rhythm: short chords on every off-beat, or chords that start a sixteenth after each beat and stop before the next one. Today pads hold one chord per bar, so there is no pumping pad at all. The verse takes use three voices, the chorus takes four, one with a sixteenth push into the next bar.

name: Open-voiced pad, half-note re-strikes
rationale: A wide, open pad voicing (fifth, third and root spread over almost two octaves, like a pianist's open-hand chord) re-struck on every half note instead of held for the whole bar. The re-strike on beat 3 follows the chord when it changes mid-bar and gives slow ballads and acoustic soul-pop a gentle pulse. The middle and slow takes alternate this voicing with a second open shape (root, fifth and a high third) so the colour shifts without new rhythm; the chorus take adds the high third and a half-quarter-quarter re-strike.

name: Divisi strings, rising top line
rationale: A four-bar string section phrase for ballad and soul-pop choruses: cellos and violas hold the lower chord tones while the first violins climb one chord tone every half bar, from the fifth up to the fifth an octave higher, so the chorus lifts towards its last bar. Every voice re-strikes on beat 3 so a mid-bar chord change is followed. The verse take keeps the shape with two voices and a slower, shorter climb; the middle take sways the top voice up and back within two bars.

name: Spiccato eighth-note ostinato
rationale: Short bowed eighth notes repeating the chord tones, the driving string ostinato of cinematic EDM drops, orchestral hip hop and modern Schlager. It gives forward motion under a vocal without competing with it. The verse take pulses on a two-note shape, the middle take rocks the top voice between the third and the root above, and the chorus takes add a low octave and, in one, a gallop rhythm (eighth plus two sixteenths).

name: Pizzicato backbeat
rationale: Plucked strings on beats 2 and 4, with a low plucked bass note on beats 1 and 3 in the fuller takes: the light oom-pah of Schlager verses and of playful acoustic pop. It is short and dry, so it leaves room for the vocal and doubles the snare. The chorus take adds an off-beat pickup before each half bar and a high root on top; the second verse take adds a skipping off-beat.

name: Legato counter-line in octaves
rationale: A slow singing counter-melody played by violins and cellos in octaves, the classic pop string line that answers the vocal between phrases. Written as a chord-tone melody it always fits the harmony, and the octave doubling never loses a voice. The verse take moves mostly in half notes, the middle take adds a dotted rhythm and a climb to the high third, and the chorus take spreads a rise and fall over four bars.

name: Salsa horn mambo hits
rationale: A salsa and Latin pop horn section (trumpets, trombone, sax) playing a mambo: short syncopated hits on the off-beats of 1 and 2 that push against the clave, answered by a falling figure where the whole close voicing steps down one inversion at a time with the trumpet leading. Latin has had to borrow ten Schlager brass patterns; these are its own idiom. The verse take keeps only the off-beat hits; the chorus takes add the falling figure and a longer held hit.

name: Soul horn stabs on 2 and 4
rationale: Short Motown and soul horn stabs on beats 2 and 4, locking with the snare: the horn section of soul-pop and of brass-driven Schlager hits. Three-note close voicing with the trumpet on top. The verse takes stab on 2 and 4 (one with an extra off-beat); the chorus takes add a pickup into each bar and a held, higher chord on the downbeat of the second bar.

name: Brass swell into a punch
rationale: A long held brass chord that builds through a bar and lands on a short punch on the next downbeat, the classic chorus lift of big-band-flavoured pop, Schlager and Latin pop. With no velocity the swell comes from the voicing climbing one inversion on beat 3 and the punch from a short, high chord followed by two off-beat kicks. The verse take is a soft, low two-note hold with no punch.

name: Schlager fanfare
rationale: A bright trumpet fanfare in parallel sixths: a quick eighth-sixteenth-sixteenth pickup on one chord and an arpeggio climbing through the chord, the festive horn call of Schlager and Volksmusik-pop intros and choruses. Sixths stay full over every chord because the two trumpets never land on the same note. The verse take is one fanfare call per two bars; the chorus take answers it with a falling reply; the middle take starts high and dips.
